nodes.title: StGit: Stacked Git - Managing Git commits as a stack of patches
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":95,"prompt":"StGit (Stacked Git) is an application for managing Git commits as a stack of patches.

Created by Catalin Marinas on July 10, 2005.

With a patch stack workflow, multiple patches can be developed concurrently and efficiently, 
with each patch focused on a single concern, resulting in both a clean Git commit history 
and improved productivity.

The tool allows developers to:
- Maintain a stack of patches on top of a branch
- Easily reorder, modify, and combine patches
- Push and pop patches from the stack
- Export patches for email submission

Original implementation was in Python. In 2022, Peter Grayson led a complete rewrite in Rust
for v2.0.0, making the tool significantly faster while maintaining the same workflow paradigm.

Timeline: July 2005 - Present (20+ years of active development)
3,598 commits across 65+ releases"}

Rewrite StGit from Python to Rust
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":95,"prompt":"After 15+ years of Python implementation (v0.4 through v1.5), the decision was made to rewrite StGit in Rust. This is the most significant architectural change in the project's history.

Key factors likely included:
- Performance improvements
- Better dependency management (static linking)
- Type safety and memory safety
- Modern tooling ecosystem (cargo)
- Long-term maintainability

The approach chosen was incremental: use pyo3 to punt unimplemented subcommands to Python implementations, progressively adding Rust implementations until no Python remains."}

nodes.title: Incremental pyo3 hybrid approach (CHOSEN)
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":95,"prompt":"The chosen approach: use pyo3 to create a Rust binary that can call out to Python implementations for unimplemented commands. Progressively replace Python code with Rust until no Python remains.

Benefits:
- Allows gradual migration with working software at each step
- Test suite remains valid throughout migration
- Can ship releases during transition
- Lower risk than full rewrite

Trade-offs:
- Temporary complexity of maintaining two languages
- Build system complexity with pyo3"}

nodes.title: Full Rust rewrite from scratch (Not chosen)
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":85,"prompt":"Alternative considered: Complete rewrite of StGit in Rust without the pyo3 bridge.

Potential benefits:
- Cleaner final architecture
- No hybrid complexity

Why not chosen:
- Higher risk of introducing regressions
- Longer time to first working version
- No releases possible during rewrite
- Test suite would need significant rework"}

nodes.title: Continue with Python (Not chosen)
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":80,"prompt":"Alternative considered: Continue maintaining and developing StGit in Python.

Benefits:
- No migration risk
- Existing codebase well understood
- Larger contributor pool familiar with Python

Why not chosen:
- Performance limitations of Python
- Dependency management challenges (pip vs system packages)
- Type safety concerns
- Desire for static binary distribution"}

nodes.title: Release v2.0.0: Complete Rust rewrite shipped!
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","commit":"a32891b4","confidence":99,"prompt":"MAJOR MILESTONE: v2.0.0 released November 6, 2022.

After 18 years of Python development (2004-2022), StGit is now 100% Rust.
- 471 commits in the Rust rewrite effort
- 7 pre-releases (2 alpha, 3 beta, 2 RC)
- ~1 year of rewrite work (October 2021 - November 2022)

Key achievements:
- Zero unsafe code in the entire codebase
- Pure Rust binary with minimal dependencies
- Improved performance and reliability
- Modern shell completion system
- Replaced stg mail with stg email format/send

Removed commands (breaking changes):
- stg clone (use git clone + stg init)
- stg mail (replaced with stg email format/send)
- stg refresh --spill (replaced with stg spill)

This marks the completion of the most significant architectural change in StGit's 20-year history."}

nodes.title: Switch from git2 to gitoxide
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":95,"prompt":"In v2.2.0, StGit switched from git2 (libgit2 bindings) to gitoxide (pure Rust git implementation).

This is a significant architectural decision:
- Aligns with the pure-Rust philosophy from the rewrite
- Removes last native dependency (libgit2)
- Potentially better performance
- Fully static binary possible

Also switched from chrono to time crate - another reduction in dependencies.

This continues the trend of simplifying the dependency tree started in the Rust rewrite."}

nodes.title: 21 years of development: 3,598 commits, 65+ releases
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":99,"prompt":"StGit is a remarkable case study in software evolution.

Timeline:
- 2004: First Python release (v0.4)
- 2004-2022: Python era (45+ releases)
- 2021-2022: Rust rewrite (1 year, 471 commits)
- 2022-2025: Rust era (35+ releases, 886 commits)

Key architectural decisions:
1. Original stacked-patch workflow design
2. Python implementation for rapid development
3. Rust rewrite for performance and reliability
4. gitoxide adoption for pure-Rust git operations

Maintenance patterns:
- Two maintainers (Catalin Marinas, Peter Grayson)
- Consistent release cadence with occasional gaps
- Strong backwards compatibility commitment
- Active user community feedback (GitHub issues)

The project demonstrates how a well-designed core concept (patch stacks) can survive and thrive through major technology transitions."}

nodes.title: Contributor pattern: Two maintainers over 21 years

{"branch":"master","confidence":95,"prompt":"StGit has had a consistent maintainer model:

- Peter Grayson: Lead developer (1863 commits), drove the Rust rewrite

Notable contributors:
- Karl Wiberg (343 commits) - significant early contributor
- Gustav Hållberg (188 commits) - stgit.el Emacs integration
- Yann Dirson (140 commits) - early development
- David Kågedal (70 commits) - Emacs integration work

Modern patterns:
- dependabot[bot] (75 commits) - automated dependency updates
- Active community contributing Emacs improvements

This two-maintainer model has proven remarkably stable, with clear succession when Peter took over primary development."}

This demonstrates commitment to editor integration as a first-class feature, not an afterthought. The fact that stgit.el survived the Python-to-Rust rewrite shows it was designed with a clean interface to the CLI."}

nodes.title: How to integrate patches with upstream mailing lists?
nodes.metadata_json:
{"branch":"master","confidence":90,"prompt":"Linux kernel development relies heavily on patch email submission. StGit needed to support the kernel workflow where patches are:
1. Developed locally as a stack
2. Formatted and sent via email to mailing lists
3. Reviewed, revised, and re-sent

This drove the need for email integration commands."}

nodes.title: How to integrate upstream changes while preserving patch stack?

Options considered:
1. Manual rebase with git rebase
2. Dedicated stg command that handles stack state

This is THE core value proposition of StGit - managing this complexity automatically."}
